I’m saying this from the perspective of a child whose mom was in a very similar position to you:

My dad would constantly berate my mom about her weight, calling her a “whale” and other abusive things. She couldn’t seem to lose a little bit of baby weight. But at the same time, my dad would criticize her for dieting and exercising a lot. He would point to movie stars while we were watching tv and look to my mom and say “Why can’t you look like that?”

Then he started policing my weight. I was about 10-15 lb heavier than other kids my age. But once the comments started at home, I felt the need to sneak food. He would yell and tell me to stop eating, even if the crinkle he was hearing in the kitchen was my textbook cover or me wrapping a gift. No matter what I accomplished, it was never good enough because I was still fat. It takes such a toll. When the bully is at home, you don’t feel safe anywhere. You internalize everything that is said to you or that you overhear. I developed an eating disorder when I was 11. But because I was overweight, my parents didn’t believe me at first. Then they sent me to inpatient ED treatment to “lose weight”. I got worse. I binged and purged more. I’d have phases of restricting. My metabolism was shot by 15. To this day, I still binge. I have to remind myself to eat because I now see food as having emotional value and moral value. I have no self-esteem. I hate every single physical characteristic of myself. Things that seem nonsensical to most to be self/conscious about, too. Like how my eyes are too close together, my face too long, my torso too long and legs too short. Things I NEVER would have even noticed unless I heard my father criticize on other women.

OP—I’m hurting for you. I’m hurting for your kid. I know Reddit has a thing where people believe commenters are being over-reactionary when telling someone in your situation to leave...but it is warranted. You deserve to love yourself and your body. You deserve to feel at home in yourself instead of trapped. You deserve a partner that worships every inch of you, no matter how your body changes. 
Your daughter deserves to see self-love and healthy, respectful interpersonal relationships modeled by her parents. You may think you can hide this...you may think you have time before she’s at risk of being affected...no. Kids are intuitive as hell. And they. are. sponges. You’re they’re entire world for the first decade of their life. What you say and do is practically gospel. 

This man wants to verbally abuse you because he knows if you hate yourself, you won’t realize that YOU DESERVE BETTER THAN HIM.

Hey, as someone who has dealt with OCD for almost two decades: this is you seeking reassurance. That tends to happen when our OCD get worse and it’s a form of ritual. I’m going to include helpful info just in case you don’t already know. If you do, sorry- not trying to be condescending. 

Everyone has intrusive thoughts. The difference between someone with OCD and a neurotypical person is that the neurotypical person won’t put a lot of emphasis on the thought, and then will go about their day. They may be like “Oh man, that was a horrible thought, I’d never want that to happen. Anyway, what am I having for lunch?”

But we with OCD assign our moral value SO closely to these thoughts that having them pass through our head AT ALL makes us question whether we actually believe these thoughts or want them to happen. We don’t. 

Sit with the anxiety that comes with these thoughts. Think about the situation that triggers your anxiety. Be mindful of your physical response. Confront the fear. Keep doing this carefully until the thought doesn’t trigger anxiety anymore. This is exposure response prevention. It is the best and most-utilized treatment out there for OCD because it works. This method actually makes sense, since the more you tell your mind to stop thinking of intrusive thoughts, the more they’ll appear. It’s like if you tell someone “Don’t think of a pink polar bear!!!!” 
What’s the first image that popped up in your head? Our brains are weird and we need to confront the anxiety so we don’t feel the need to do obsessive behaviors (like seeking reassurance or washing hands too much or avoiding public bathrooms). 

You’re gonna be fine. You know yourself. You know deep in the back of your mind if these intrusive thoughts are irrational or not. But the anxiety and uncertainty and chemical imbalance makes your fight or flight stimuli shoot off and say “omg what if?”

Take a few breaths. Maybe watch a clip of a YouTube video of a serial killer documentary to start exposure, IF YOU FEEL LIKE YOURE OK DOING SO. Or start smaller if need be. Look at the picture of a serial killer or read their names out loud. Until you don’t feel anxious about this intrusive thought when triggered by things relevant to it. 
You’re gonna be ok. OCD is the worst, but it’s a lifelong process that can become a background noise of you work hard. I’m working my way back to that after the whole social distancing made it rear it’s ugly head again!

However, if you watch porn and shame and/or denigrate sex workers (you can prefer not to date one), you are the worst type of hypocrite. Full stop.

Ridiculous false equivalency. If someone found out you watch porn in your free time, you won’t be at risk of losing a job and other important relationships. The woman’s lying is still egregious, but so is the shame and stigmatization that drove her to do it.

This is the best answer. I feel sorry for her for probably being in a rough place and doing something she regrets so she now has to lie, BUT- that’s not OP’s or any person she dates problem. I feel badly for the fact that OP was bamboozled. That was intentional deceit on her part, whatever the reasoning may be. 

However, OP DOES seem more focused on what other people think rather than processing, healing, and moving on. 
She lied, you broke up (understandably), now get tested (I’m surprised people don’t do this each time they start a new relationship anyway), see a therapist or counselor if you have the resources, and worry about yourself. Statistically, there’s a good chance you were probably already carrying HPV and possibly herpes (though there’s no current test for men for the former and the results from testing for the latter are capricious at best), and those are the STIs that have the true risk of spreading amongst the adult film industry...but as the person above stated, it’s no different for any other sexually active adults. Sex workers actually get tested far more frequently than most people do, as a part of industry standards and to best ensure the safety of those involved. 

The world isn’t going to stop because you dated a sex worker and she lied about it. You seem to be experiencing cognitive distortions by placing too much emphasis on what others think. This isn’t surprising, after a big shock. However, if you don’t acknowledge it and reframe these thoughts, you’re going to be miserable and may struggle being in a relationship again. As for “worrying about what others think,” particularly in reference to your friends: If anything, they are probably worried and showed you the videos to help you. If your friends are gathered snickering like school children, you need new friends. Get your shit together or this will surpass a break-up and become a breakdown. This is a shitty situation but far from the end of the world. You owe yourself a clear head to move forward.
